claims.source: These approaches revealed lrp4 expression in both olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) and projection neurons (PNs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by intersectional genetic strategies showing expression in ORNs.

claims.claim: lrp4 is expressed in projection neurons (PNs).
claims.source: These approaches revealed lrp4 expression in both olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) and projection neurons (PNs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by intersectional genetic strategies showing expression in PNs.

claims.claim: LRP4 localizes to synaptic neuropil regions.
claims.source: LRP4 localizes to synaptic neuropil regions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by expansion microscopy showing LRP4 localization in synaptic regions.

claims.claim: LRP4 localizes either coincidentally with Bruchpilot or to the space adjacent to active zones.
claims.source: Within individual expanded glomeruli of proExM-treated brains, LRP4 and Brp localized to similar regions (Figure 1E) and, when examined at high magnification, LRP4 localized either coincidentally with Brp (Figure 1F, arrowhead) or to the space adjacent to active zones (Figure 1F, arrow).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by expansion microscopy showing LRP4 localization relative to Bruchpilot.

claims.claim: LRP4 localization is similar to that of known synaptic organizers.
claims.source: This combination of active zone and periactive zone localization is similar to that of known synaptic organizers (Jepson et al., 2014; Li et al., 2007; Mosca et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published localization patterns of other synaptic organizers.

claims.claim: 99.5% of lrp4-positive cells express the neuronal marker ELAV.
claims.source: Nearly all lrp4-positive cells observed (99.5%) expressed the neuronal marker ELAV (Robinow and White, 1988) (Figure 1G), indicating that these cells were neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization between lrp4 and ELAV.

claims.claim: 0.4% of lrp4-positive cells express the glial marker Repo.
claims.source: Few (0.4%) expressed the glial marker Repo (Xiong et al., 1994) (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization between lrp4 and Repo.

claims.claim: 59.1% of lrp4-positive cells express choline acetyltransferase (ChAT).
claims.source: The majority of lrp4-positive cells (59.1%) also expressed choline acetyltransferase (ChAT; Figure 1I), a marker for cholinergic excitatory neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization between lrp4 and ChAT.

claims.claim: 22.4% of lrp4-positive cells express vGlut.
claims.source: We also observed partial overlap between lrp4-positive neurons and vGlut (22.4%; Figure 1J), the vesicular transporter for glutamate.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization between lrp4 and vGlut.

claims.claim: 0.3% of lrp4-positive cells express GABA.
claims.source: Interestingly, there was little overlap (0.3%) between lrp4 and GABA, the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in Drosophila (Figure 1K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of colocalization between lrp4 and GABA.

claims.claim: LRP4 is expressed at synaptic terminals of a subset of excitatory cholinergic neurons.
claims.source: Thus, LRP4 is expressed at synaptic terminals of a subset of excitatory cholinergic neurons and a subset of glutamatergic neurons that may be excitatory or inhibitory, but is excluded from inhibitory GABAergic neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization data with neurotransmitter markers.

claims.claim: LRP4 is expressed at synaptic terminals of a subset of glutamatergic neurons that may be excitatory or inhibitory.
claims.source: Thus, LRP4 is expressed at synaptic terminals of a subset of excitatory cholinergic neurons and a subset of glutamatergic neurons that may be excitatory or inhibitory, but is excluded from inhibitory GABAergic neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization data with neurotransmitter markers.

claims.claim: LRP4 is excluded from inhibitory GABAergic neurons.
claims.source: Thus, LRP4 is expressed at synaptic terminals of a subset of excitatory cholinergic neurons and a subset of glutamatergic neurons that may be excitatory or inhibitory, but is excluded from inhibitory GABAergic neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization data showing minimal overlap with GABA.

claims.claim: lrp4dalek mutants show a 31% reduction in the number of Brp-Short puncta in VA1v ORN axon terminals compared to control adults.
claims.source: In ORN axon terminals projecting to the VA1v glomerulus in males (Figure 2B), lrp4dalek mutants (Figure 2C,H) showed a 31% reduction in the number of puncta for Brp-Short, an active zone marker, compared to control adults (Figure 2B,H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in mutants versus controls.

claims.claim: The reduction in Brp-Short puncta in lrp4dalek mutants is recapitulated by expressing RNAi against lrp4 only in ORNs.
claims.source: This phenotype was recapitulated when we expressed any of four independent transgenic RNAi constructs against lrp4 only in ORNs (Figure 2D,H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that LRP4 functions presynaptically in regulating active zone number.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments showing similar phenotypes to the null mutant.

claims.claim: LRP4 functions presynaptically in regulating active zone number.
claims.source: This phenotype was recapitulated when we expressed any of four independent transgenic RNAi constructs against lrp4 only in ORNs (Figure 2D,H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that LRP4 functions presynaptically in regulating active zone number.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell-autonomous RNAi experiments in presynaptic neurons.

claims.claim: lrp4 loss-of-function has no effect on neurite volume in ORNs.
claims.source: These changes were independent of glomerular volume: lrp4 loss-of-function had no effect on neurite volume (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of neurite volume showing no change.

claims.claim: Loss of lrp4 decreases Dα7-EGFP puncta numbers by 29% in PN dendrites compared to controls.
claims.source: Loss of lrp4 decreased Dα7-EGFP puncta numbers by 29% compared to controls (Figure 2F–G,I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of postsynaptic receptor puncta.

claims.claim: The postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor deficit in lrp4 mutants is independent of neurite volume.
claims.source: This deficit was also independent of neurite volume (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), again demonstrating that lrp4 perturbation phenotypes did not result from decreased neuronal projection size.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification showing no change in neurite volume.

claims.claim: LRP4 overexpression in ORNs increases the number of Brp-Short puncta by 30%.
claims.source: LRP4 overexpression increased the number of Brp-Short puncta by 30% (Figure 2E,H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2); this increase was also independent of neurite volume (Figure 2h and Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3) as the glomeruli remained the same size.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in overexpression conditions.

claims.claim: The increase in Brp-Short puncta from LRP4 overexpression is independent of neurite volume.
claims.source: LRP4 overexpression increased the number of Brp-Short puncta by 30% (Figure 2E,H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2); this increase was also independent of neurite volume (Figure 2h and Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3) as the glomeruli remained the same size.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification showing no change in glomerular volume.

claims.claim: There is a direct relationship between presynaptic LRP4 expression and synapse number in excitatory neurons.
claims.source: Thus, there is a direct relationship between presynaptic LRP4 expression and synapse number in excitatory neurons: removing LRP4 reduces, while overexpressing LRP4 increases, synapse number.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments showing opposite effects.

claims.claim: lrp4dalek mutants show a 31% reduction in T-bar profiles per terminal in putative ORN terminals.
claims.source: T-bar profiles were evident in both genotypes, but were reduced in number by 31% in mutant terminals (Figure 3C), which exactly matched the reduction observed by Brp-Short puncta measurements (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy quantification of T-bar profiles.

claims.claim: Terminal perimeter is slightly but significantly increased in lrp4dalek terminals.
claims.source: Terminal perimeter was slightly but significantly increased in lrp4dalek terminals (Figure 3D), resulting in a 36% reduction in T-bar density when compared to control (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy measurements of terminal perimeter.

claims.claim: lrp4dalek mutants show a 36% reduction in T-bar density compared to control.
claims.source: Terminal perimeter was slightly but significantly increased in lrp4dalek terminals (Figure 3D), resulting in a 36% reduction in T-bar density when compared to control (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy quantification of T-bar density.

claims.claim: LRP4 is necessary for the proper number of synapses in putative ORN terminals of the antennal lobe.
claims.source: These results are consistent with those observed via confocal microscopy, and demonstrate that LRP4 is necessary for the proper number of synapses in putative ORN terminals of the antennal lobe.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data confirming light microscopy findings.

claims.claim: The majority of T-bars in lrp4 mutants display one or more morphological defects.
claims.source: However, whereas irregular T-bars in control animals were rare (<5% of total T-bars), the majority of T-bars in lrp4 mutants displayed one or more defects (Figure 3L–Q), including immature T-bars that lacked tops (Figure 3L), detached T-bars (Figure 3M), misshapen T-bars of varying configurations and aggregations (Figure 3N–P), and multiple T-bars beyond those observed in control animals (Figure 3Q).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy showing various T-bar morphology defects.

claims.claim: LRP4 is required for individual active zones to assume normal morphology, attach to the membrane, and have proper spacing.
claims.source: Thus, in addition to controlling the number of synapses, LRP4 is also required for individual active zones to assume normal morphology, attach to the membrane, and have proper spacing.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy showing multiple types of T-bar defects.

claims.claim: Loss of lrp4 in GABAergic inhibitory neurons does not affect synapse number.
claims.source: When LRP4 function was impaired using the lrp4dalek mutant or RNAi in these neurons, synapse number was unaffected (Figure 4A–B,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in inhibitory neurons.

claims.claim: The reduction of synapse number under LRP4 loss-of-function conditions is specific for excitatory neurons.
claims.source: Thus, the reduction of synapse number under LRP4 loss-of-function conditions appeared specific for excitatory neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparing effects in excitatory versus inhibitory neurons.

claims.claim: LRP4 overexpression in inhibitory neurons increases synapse number by 35%.
claims.source: Interestingly, when LRP4 was overexpressed in inhibitory neurons, we observed a 35% increase in synapse number without an accompanying change in neurite volume, similar to what we observed for excitatory neurons (Figure 4C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in inhibitory neurons overexpressing LRP4.

claims.claim: Inhibitory GABAergic neurons possess the downstream machinery necessary for LRP4 to function in adding synapses.
claims.source: This suggests that, while inhibitory GABAergic neurons do not normally utilize LRP4 to regulate synapse number, they possess the downstream machinery necessary for LRP4 to function in adding synapses.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the gain-of-function phenotype in inhibitory neurons.

claims.claim: Excitatory and inhibitory neurons likely use distinct cell surface synaptic organizers that converge on common mechanisms for synapse addition.
claims.source: As such, excitatory and inhibitory neurons likely use distinct cell surface synaptic organizers (LRP4 for excitatory neurons) that converge on common mechanisms for synapse addition.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential requirement but shared competency for LRP4 function.

claims.claim: Loss of lrp4 in excitatory projection neurons reduces synapse number in the lateral horn by 40%.
claims.source: In lrp4 mutants, the number of excitatory lateral horn synapses was reduced by 40%, consistent with a role for LRP4 in synapse formation (Figure 5B–C,F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in lateral horn projection neurons.

claims.claim: PN perturbation of lrp4 using RNAi reduces synapse number in the lateral horn similarly to the loss-of-function allele.
claims.source: PN perturbation of lrp4 using RNAi reduced synapse number similarly to the loss-of-function allele, demonstrating a presynaptic role for lrp4 in these neurons (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments showing similar phenotypes to the null mutant.

claims.claim: Perturbation of lrp4 in Mz699-positive inhibitory projection neurons has no effect on the number of synapses.
claims.source: Perturbation of lrp4 in Mz699-positive iPNs, however, had no effect on the number of synapses (Figure 5D–E,G, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) despite a slight reduction in neurite volume in lrp4dalek mutants (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in inhibitory projection neurons.

claims.claim: LRP4 overexpression in Mz699-positive neurons increases synapse number.
claims.source: Despite a lack of a loss-of-function phenotype, we observed an increase in synapse number when we overexpressed LRP4-HA in Mz699-positive neurons (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in inhibitory projection neurons overexpressing LRP4.

claims.claim: LRP4 has a general role in promoting excitatory synapse number.
claims.source: Thus, the results of lrp4 perturbation on excitatory and inhibitory synapses in the lateral horn resembled those of the antennal lobe, suggesting a general role for LRP4 in promoting excitatory synapse number.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from similar phenotypes observed in multiple brain regions.

claims.claim: Flies expressing lrp4 RNAi in ORNs exhibit a near complete abrogation of attractive behavior to apple cider vinegar.
claims.source: Flies bearing both transgenes (and thus, reduced lrp4 expression) exhibited a near complete abrogation of attractive behavior and were no longer able to distinguish the attractive apple cider vinegar from a water control (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay quantification.

claims.claim: Presynaptic LRP4 in ORNs is necessary for normal olfactory attraction behavior.
claims.source: Thus, presynaptic LRP4 in ORNs is necessary for normal olfactory attraction behavior.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral defects following ORN-specific LRP4 knockdown.

claims.claim: Simultaneous knockdown of GABABR2 and lrp4 in ORNs markedly suppresses the behavioral phenotype associated with lrp4 knockdown alone.
claims.source: Simultaneous knockdown of GABABR2 and lrp4, however, markedly suppressed the behavioral phenotype associated with lrp4 knockdown alone (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay showing rescue of the phenotype.

claims.claim: Olfactory attraction behavior requires a proper level of net excitatory drive in the antennal lobe circuit.
claims.source: These results suggest that olfactory attraction behavior requires a proper level of net excitatory drive in the antennal lobe circuit and that defects caused by weakened excitatory synapses can be compensated for by reducing inhibition.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral suppression by reducing inhibition.

claims.claim: Loss of lrp4 results in improper axonal accumulations of Bruchpilot in larval transverse nerves.
claims.source: However, in lrp4dalek mutants, Bruchpilot improperly accumulated in the transverse nerves (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry showing Bruchpilot accumulation in nerves.

claims.claim: Loss of srpk79D results in improper axonal accumulations of Bruchpilot in larval transverse nerves.
claims.source: This kind of accumulation is rarely observed in wild type, but is also most notably associated with loss of SRPK79D (Figure 7C), a conserved serine-arginine protein kinase that localizes to NMJ terminals and negatively regulates premature active zone assembly before Bruchpilot reaches the fly NMJ (Johnson et al., 2009; Nieratschker et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and published data on SRPK79D function.

claims.claim: Brp accumulation in lrp4 and srpk79D mutants is not accompanied by focal accumulations of Synaptotagmin I.
claims.source: In both lrp4 and srpk79D mutants, Brp accumulation was not accompanied by focal accumulations of Synaptotagmin I, indicating that axonal trafficking is not generally impaired (Figure 7A–C) (Gindhart et al., 1998; Johnson et al., 2009; Nieratschker et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry showing absence of Synaptotagmin I accumulation.

claims.claim: Venus-SRPK79D largely colocalizes with Brp-Short in ORN terminals.
claims.source: When expressed only in VA1v ORNs, venus-SRPK79D localized to axon terminals and overlapped with Brp-Short, demonstrating localization with and adjacent to CNS active zones (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy showing colocalization.

claims.claim: LRP4-HA and venus-SRPK79D exhibit coincident and adjacent localization in ORNs.
claims.source: In the ORNs of expanded individual glomeruli, LRP4-HA and venus-SRPK79D exhibited coincident and adjacent localization (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by expansion microscopy showing spatial relationship.

claims.claim: Loss of lrp4 reduces synaptic SRPK79D levels by approximately 50%.
claims.source: We also examined this synaptic localization in lrp4dalek mutants: loss of lrp4 reduced synaptic SRPK79D levels by ~50% (Figure 7F–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of venus-SRPK79D fluorescence in mutants.

claims.claim: LRP4 is necessary for the proper localization and/or expression of SRPK79D.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that LRP4 is necessary for the proper localization and / or expression of SRPK79D and suggest that SRPK79D might act downstream of LRP4 to regulate synapse number.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reduced SRPK79D levels in lrp4 mutants.

claims.claim: LRP4 and SRPK79D are close enough to interact as shown by proximity ligation assays.
claims.source: However, in the presence of both transgenes and the appropriate probes (Figure 7J and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D), we detected positive signal indicating that the proteins were close enough to interact.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proximity ligation assay showing positive signal.

claims.claim: Reducing srpk79D function presynaptically results in a 15% reduction in the number of Brp-Short puncta.
claims.source: First, reducing srpk79D function presynaptically using an established RNAi (Johnson et al., 2009) expressed in VA1v ORNs resulted in a 15% reduction in the number of Brp-Short puncta compared to control (Figure 8A–B,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta following RNAi knockdown.

claims.claim: SRPK79D is required for normal CNS synapse number.
claims.source: Thus, SRPK79D is required for normal CNS synapse number.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the reduction in synapse number following srpk79D knockdown.

claims.claim: Concurrent removal of one copy each of lrp4 and srpk79D results in a significant reduction in Brp-Short puncta.
claims.source: However, when one copy of each was concurrently removed, we observed a significant reduction in Brp-Short puncta (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments showing synergistic effects.

claims.claim: LRP4 and SRPK79D function in the same genetic pathway.
claims.source: This suggests that the two function in the same genetic pathway and may work together to ensure proper synapse number.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic interaction data.

claims.claim: Presynaptic overexpression of SRPK79D partially suppresses the synaptic phenotype associated with the lrp4dalek mutation.
claims.source: Presynaptic overexpression of SRPK79D in VA1v ORNs partially suppressed the synaptic phenotype associated with the lrp4dalek mutation, resulting in 92% of the normal number of synapses (Figure 8A,C–E), whereas overexpression of SRPK79D in a wild-type background had no effect (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Brp-Short puncta in rescue experiments.

claims.claim: LRP4 requires SRPK79D to mediate its overexpression phenotype.
claims.source: When LRP4 was overexpressed concurrently with srpk79D RNAi, the phenotype resembled that of srpk79D RNAi alone (Figure 8E). This suggests that LRP4 requires SRPK79D to mediate its overexpression phenotype, likely by functioning through SRPK79D to increase the number of synapses.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by epistasis experiments showing SRPK79D is required for LRP4 overexpression effects.

claims.claim: LRP4 and SRPK79D closely interact presynaptically in the same genetic pathway to ensure the proper number of excitatory synapses.
claims.source: Combined, these indicate that LRP4 and SRPK79D closely interact presynaptically in the same genetic pathway to ensure the proper number of excitatory synapses.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple genetic interaction and epistasis experiments.

claims.claim: Flies expressing srpk79D RNAi in all ORNs demonstrate a nearly complete abrogation of attraction behavior.
claims.source: Flies expressing srpk79D RNAi in all ORNs demonstrated a nearly complete abrogation of attraction behavior (Figure 8F) that was indistinguishable from the lrp4 RNAi phenotype.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay quantification.

claims.claim: SRPK79D overexpression partially suppresses the lrp4 loss-of-function behavioral phenotype.
claims.source: Driving both SRPK79D overexpression and lrp4 RNAi in all ORNs, however, resulted in a partial suppression of the behavioral phenotype associated with lrp4 RNAi (Figure 8F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay showing rescue of the phenotype.

claims.claim: SRPK79D is likely a key downstream effector of LRP4 in regulating synapse number and olfactory attraction behavior.
claims.source: As the synaptic level of SRPK79D is positively regulated by LRP4 and SRPK79D overexpression suppresses the morphological and functional phenotypes associated with lrp4 loss-of-function, SRPK79D is likely a key downstream effector of LRP4 in regulating synapse number and thus, normal olfactory attraction behavior.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic and functional relationships between LRP4 and SRPK79D.

claims.claim: LRP4 is a synaptic protein whose expression may be preferential for excitatory neurons in the Drosophila CNS.
claims.source: This study identifies LRP4 as a synaptic protein whose expression may be preferential for excitatory neurons in the Drosophila CNS (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis and colocalization with neurotransmitter markers.

claims.claim: LRP4 functions presynaptically to regulate the number of active zones in presynaptic ORNs.
claims.source: In the Drosophila CNS, LRP4 functions presynaptically to regulate the number of active zones in presynaptic ORNs (Figures 2–3) and acetylcholine receptor clusters in the PNs postsynaptic to those ORNs (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell-autonomous manipulation experiments.

claims.claim: LRP4 controls the morphology of individual active zones.
claims.source: Moreover, LRP4 also controls the morphology of individual active zones: lrp4 mutant T-bars exhibit striking defects in patterning and biogenesis (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy showing T-bar morphology defects.

claims.claim: LRP4 defects are specific for excitatory neurons.
claims.source: These defects are specific for excitatory neurons, as inhibitory neuron synapses in the antennal lobe remain unaffected (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparing effects in excitatory versus inhibitory neurons.

claims.claim: LRP4 overexpression can increase synapse number cell autonomously in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
claims.source: Overexpression of LRP4, however, can increase synapse number cell autonomously in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Figures 2–4), suggesting that both share common mechanisms for synapse addition.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gain-of-function experiments in both neuron types.

claims.claim: The role for LRP4 extends to higher order olfactory neuropil in the lateral horn.
claims.source: The role for LRP4 further extends to higher order olfactory neuropil in the lateral horn (Figure 5), suggesting that it may serve a general role in synaptic organization.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by similar phenotypes observed in multiple brain regions.

claims.claim: Perturbation of LRP4 in excitatory ORNs abrogates olfactory attraction behavior.
claims.source: Underscoring the functional importance of LRP4, its perturbation in excitatory ORNs abrogated olfactory attraction behavior (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assays showing loss of attraction.

claims.claim: A proper level of excitatory drive is important for functional circuit output.
claims.source: The suppression of the behavioral phenotype by reducing presynaptic inhibition onto ORNs further suggests that a proper level of excitatory drive is important for functional circuit output.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral rescue by reducing inhibition.

claims.claim: LRP4 likely functions through SRPK79D to mediate both morphological and behavioral effects.
claims.source: To mediate both morphological and behavioral effects, LRP4 likely functions through SRPK79D, a conserved SR-protein kinase whose loss-of-function phenotypes resemble those of lrp4 (Figures 7–8), whose synaptic localization depends on LRP4 (Figure 7), who interacts genetically with and is physically in proximity to LRP4 (Figures 7–8), and whose overexpression suppresses the phenotypes associated with loss of lrp4 (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of genetic and molecular evidence.

claims.claim: At the vertebrate neuromuscular junction, LRP4 forms a receptor complex with MuSK in muscle fibers to promote clustering of acetylcholine receptors in response to motoneuron-derived agrin.
claims.source: At the vertebrate neuromuscular junction, one of these critical organizers is LRP4. There, it forms a receptor complex with MuSK in muscle fibers to promote clustering of acetylcholine receptors in response to motoneuron-derived agrin (Zhang et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2008; Weatherbee et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Muscle LRP4 can function as a retrograde signal with an unknown motoneuron receptor to regulate presynaptic differentiation.
claims.source: Muscle LRP4 can also function as a retrograde signal with an unknown motoneuron receptor to regulate presynaptic differentiation (Yumoto et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Motoneuron-derived LRP4 can regulate presynaptic differentiation, demonstrating a role for neuronal LRP4.
claims.source: First, motoneuron-derived LRP4 can regulate presynaptic differentiation, demonstrating a role for neuronal LRP4 (Wu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: In the vertebrate central nervous system, agrin is not essential for synapse formation.
claims.source: Second, in the vertebrate central nervous system (CNS), agrin is not essential for synapse formation (Daniels, 2012) though LRP4 can regulate synaptic plasticity, development, and cognitive function (Gomez et al., 2014; Pohlkamp et al., 2015), through functioning in astrocytes in some cases (Sun et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: LRP4 can regulate synaptic plasticity, development, and cognitive function in the vertebrate CNS.
claims.source: Second, in the vertebrate central nervous system (CNS), agrin is not essential for synapse formation (Daniels, 2012) though LRP4 can regulate synaptic plasticity, development, and cognitive function (Gomez et al., 2014; Pohlkamp et al., 2015), through functioning in astrocytes in some cases (Sun et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: The Drosophila genome contains an LRP4 homologue, but no clear agrin or MuSK homologues.
claims.source: In this vein, the Drosophila genome contains an LRP4 homologue, but no clear agrin or MuSK homologues (Adams et al., 2000), so any role for LRP4 there must be agrin-independent.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to genome annotation.

claims.claim: Any role for LRP4 in Drosophila must be agrin-independent.
claims.source: In this vein, the Drosophila genome contains an LRP4 homologue, but no clear agrin or MuSK homologues (Adams et al., 2000), so any role for LRP4 there must be agrin-independent.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of agrin and MuSK homologues in Drosophila.

claims.claim: LRP4 functions largely through the conserved, presynaptic SR-protein kinase, SRPK79D.
claims.source: LRP4 functions largely through the conserved, presynaptic SR-protein kinase, SRPK79D.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic and molecular interaction data.

claims.claim: LRP4 and SRPK79D interact genetically and epistatically.
claims.source: LRP4 and SRPK79D interact genetically and epistatically, as SRPK79D overexpression can suppress lrp4-related phenotypes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction and epistasis experiments.

claims.claim: The role for LRP4 occurs preferentially in excitatory neurons.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, this role for LRP4 occurs preferentially in excitatory neurons, as impairing lrp4 in inhibitory neurons has no effect.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by differential effects in excitatory versus inhibitory neurons.

claims.claim: LRP4 may represent a conserved synaptic organizer that functions presynaptically, cell autonomously, and independently of agrin to coordinate synapse number and function.
claims.source: Thus, LRP4 may represent a conserved synaptic organizer that functions presynaptically, cell autonomously, and independently of agrin to coordinate synapse number and function.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary inference from all the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: lrp4dalek mutants are viable with a slightly reduced body size.
claims.source: lrp4dalek mutants were viable with a slightly reduced body size.
claims.evidence: The claim is an observation from maintaining mutant stocks.

claims.claim: Protein retention expansion microscopy achieves approximately 4-fold isotropic expansion of Drosophila CNS tissue.
claims.source: Using protein-retention expansion microscopy (proExM), we obtained reliable, ~4 fold isotropic expansion of Drosophila CNS tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from expansion microscopy experiments.

claims.claim: SRPK79D is a conserved serine-arginine protein kinase that localizes to NMJ terminals and negatively regulates premature active zone assembly before Bruchpilot reaches the fly NMJ.
claims.source: This kind of accumulation is rarely observed in wild type, but is also most notably associated with loss of SRPK79D (Figure 7C), a conserved serine-arginine protein kinase that localizes to NMJ terminals and negatively regulates premature active zone assembly before Bruchpilot reaches the fly NMJ (Johnson et al., 2009; Nieratschker et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Distinct ALS and MG populations are seropositive for LRP4 autoantibodies.
claims.source: Distinct ALS and MG populations are seropositive for LRP4 autoantibodies (Tsivgoulis et al., 2014; Tzartos et al., 2014) and double seronegative for Agrin or MuSK, suggesting that seropositivity is not a byproduct of generalized NMJ breakdown.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Injection of LRP4 function-blocking antibodies into mice recapitulates myasthenia gravis.
claims.source: Further, injection of LRP4 function-blocking antibodies into mice recapitulates MG (Shen et al., 2013).

results.result: CG8909 is identified as the Drosophila LRP4 homologue, sharing 38% overall identity with human LRP4, with higher conservation in the extracellular LDL-repeat region (61%) and lower conservation in the intracellular tail (28%).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are supported by sequence alignment data and domain organization analysis presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The identification is based on bioinformatic analysis showing significant sequence homology, particularly in functionally important extracellular domains.

results.result: LRP4 is broadly expressed throughout the adult Drosophila brain, including the antennal lobes, optic lobes, mushroom body, and lateral horn, with enrichment in synaptic neuropil regions. Antibody specificity is validated by complete loss of signal in lrp4 deletion mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C11 are well-supported by multiple complementary approaches including antibody staining, GAL4-driven reporter expression, and validation in null mutants (Figure 1B-D). The consistency across methods and the negative control in mutants provide strong evidence for the expression pattern.

results.result: lrp4 is expressed in both olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) and projection neurons (PNs) as demonstrated by intersectional genetic strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 are supported by intersectional genetic approaches using FLP-FRT systems with cell-type-specific drivers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E). The use of independent drivers for ORNs and PNs provides convincing evidence for expression in both cell types.

results.result: LRP4 localizes to synaptic neuropil regions, either coincident with or adjacent to the active zone marker Bruchpilot, similar to known synaptic organizers.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figure 1E-F) showing LRP4 localization relative to Bruchpilot at high resolution. The comparison to known synaptic organizers (C16) is appropriately cited and provides context for the localization pattern.

results.result: LRP4 is predominantly expressed in neurons (99.5% ELAV-positive), with minimal glial expression (0.4% Repo-positive). Among neurons, LRP4 is expressed in excitatory cholinergic neurons (59.1% ChAT-positive) and a subset of glutamatergic neurons (22.4% vGlut-positive), but is largely excluded from inhibitory GABAergic neurons (0.3% GABA-positive).
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C24 are supported by systematic colocalization analysis with cell-type markers (Figure 1G-K). The quantification is rigorous (n=8 animals, ≥200 cells per animal) and the pattern of expression is consistent with the functional specificity for excitatory neurons demonstrated later in the manuscript.

results.result: Loss of lrp4 in ORNs reduces the number of Brp-Short puncta by 31% without affecting neurite volume, demonstrating that LRP4 functions presynaptically to regulate active zone number.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 are strongly supported by both null mutant analysis and cell-autonomous RNAi experiments using four independent RNAi lines (Figure 2B-D,H and supplements). The consistency across multiple genetic manipulations and the independence from neurite volume changes provide robust evidence for a specific presynaptic role in synapse number regulation.

results.result: Loss of lrp4 decreases postsynaptic Dα7-EGFP acetylcholine receptor puncta by 29% in PN dendrites, independent of neurite volume.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 are supported by quantification of postsynaptic receptor puncta (Figure 2F-G,I). The magnitude of the postsynaptic effect matches the presynaptic phenotype, though the authors appropriately note they cannot exclude an additional postsynaptic role for LRP4.

results.result: LRP4 overexpression in ORNs increases Brp-Short puncta by 30% without affecting neurite volume, demonstrating a direct relationship between presynaptic LRP4 expression and synapse number.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 are supported by gain-of-function experiments (Figure 2E,H). The bidirectional effects (loss-of-function reduces, gain-of-function increases synapse number) provide strong evidence for LRP4's instructive role in synapse formation.

results.result: Electron microscopy confirms that lrp4 mutants show a 31% reduction in T-bar profiles per terminal and a 36% reduction in T-bar density, validating that LRP4 is necessary for proper synapse number in ORN terminals.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 are supported by rigorous TEM analysis with large sample sizes (2688 control terminals, 3123 mutant terminals from multiple animals, Figure 3A-E). The EM data independently confirms the light microscopy findings and provides ultrastructural validation.

results.result: The majority of T-bars in lrp4 mutants display morphological defects including immature T-bars lacking tops, detached T-bars, misshapen T-bars, and abnormal T-bar aggregations, demonstrating that LRP4 is required for proper active zone morphology, membrane attachment, and spacing.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by detailed EM analysis showing multiple types of T-bar defects (Figure 3L-Q). The qualitative observation that the majority of mutant T-bars show defects (compared to <5% in controls) is striking, though quantification of the frequency of each defect type would strengthen the claim.

results.result: Loss of lrp4 in GABAergic inhibitory neurons does not affect synapse number, demonstrating that the requirement for LRP4 in synapse formation is specific to excitatory neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 are supported by experiments in GAD1-positive inhibitory neurons showing no change in Brp-Short puncta with lrp4 loss-of-function (Figure 4A-B,D). This cell-type specificity is consistent with the expression pattern and provides important mechanistic insight.

results.result: LRP4 overexpression in inhibitory neurons increases synapse number by 35%, suggesting that while inhibitory neurons don't normally use LRP4, they possess the downstream machinery for LRP4-mediated synapse addition, indicating that excitatory and inhibitory neurons use distinct organizers converging on common mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by gain-of-function experiments in inhibitory neurons (Figure 4C-D). The interpretation that inhibitory neurons possess competency for LRP4 function despite not normally expressing it is reasonable, though the claim about distinct organizers converging on common mechanisms (C44) is somewhat speculative.

results.result: In the lateral horn, loss of lrp4 reduces excitatory projection neuron synapse number by 40% but has no effect on inhibitory projection neuron synapses, while LRP4 overexpression increases synapse number in both cell types, suggesting a general role for LRP4 in promoting excitatory synapse number across brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 are supported by analysis in a second brain region (Figure 5). The consistency of the phenotype across different brain regions (antennal lobe and lateral horn) strengthens the conclusion that LRP4 has a general role in excitatory synapse formation.

results.result: Presynaptic LRP4 in ORNs is necessary for normal olfactory attraction behavior, and the behavioral deficit can be suppressed by reducing presynaptic inhibition via GABABR2 knockdown, suggesting that proper excitatory drive is required for functional circuit output.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 are supported by behavioral assays (Figure 6). The genetic suppression by reducing inhibition provides functional insight, though the authors appropriately note that the morphological phenotype is not rescued, suggesting the remaining synapses may be functionally impaired.

results.result: Loss of lrp4 or srpk79D results in improper axonal accumulations of Bruchpilot in larval transverse nerves without general trafficking defects, as Synaptotagmin I does not accumulate.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by immunohistochemistry in larval nerves (Figure 7A-C). The similarity between lrp4 and srpk79D phenotypes provides initial evidence for a functional relationship, and the absence of Synaptotagmin I accumulation appropriately rules out general trafficking defects.

results.result: Venus-SRPK79D colocalizes with Brp-Short in ORN terminals and exhibits coincident and adjacent localization with LRP4-HA. Loss of lrp4 reduces synaptic SRPK79D levels by approximately 50%, demonstrating that LRP4 is necessary for proper SRPK79D localization and/or expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by confocal and expansion microscopy showing colocalization (Figure 7D-E) and quantification of SRPK79D levels in mutants (Figure 7F-H). The reduction in SRPK79D levels in lrp4 mutants provides strong evidence for a functional relationship.

results.result: LRP4 and SRPK79D are close enough to interact as demonstrated by proximity ligation assays.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 is supported by PLA experiments (Figure 7I-J and supplement). The positive PLA signal indicates the proteins are within 30-40 nm, suggesting potential physical interaction, though PLA does not prove direct binding.

results.result: SRPK79D is required for normal CNS synapse number (15% reduction with RNAi), and genetic interaction experiments show that concurrent removal of one copy each of lrp4 and srpk79D results in significant synapse reduction, suggesting they function in the same genetic pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65 are supported by loss-of-function and genetic interaction experiments (Figure 8A-B,E and supplement). The transheterozygote interaction provides evidence for functioning in the same pathway, though the effect is modest.

results.result: SRPK79D overexpression partially suppresses the lrp4 synaptic phenotype (restoring to 92% of normal), and LRP4 requires SRPK79D for its overexpression phenotype, demonstrating that LRP4 and SRPK79D interact presynaptically in the same genetic pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by epistasis experiments (Figure 8A,C-E). The suppression of lrp4 phenotypes by SRPK79D overexpression and the requirement for SRPK79D in LRP4 overexpression effects provide strong evidence for SRPK79D functioning downstream of LRP4.

results.result: SRPK79D knockdown in ORNs abolishes olfactory attraction behavior, and SRPK79D overexpression partially suppresses the lrp4 behavioral phenotype, indicating that SRPK79D is a key downstream effector of LRP4 in regulating synapse number and olfactory behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by behavioral assays (Figure 8F). The parallel between morphological and behavioral suppression by SRPK79D overexpression strengthens the conclusion that SRPK79D is a key downstream effector.

results.result: LRP4 is a synaptic protein preferentially expressed in excitatory neurons that functions presynaptically to regulate active zone number and morphology in a cell-type-specific manner across multiple brain regions, with functional consequences for olfactory behavior, likely acting through SRPK79D.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C80 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing results from expression analysis, loss- and gain-of-function experiments, ultrastructural analysis, behavioral assays, and mechanistic studies. These conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Prior work has established LRP4's role at the vertebrate NMJ in the agrin-MuSK pathway and in vertebrate CNS function, while Drosophila lacks clear agrin and MuSK homologues, indicating any Drosophila LRP4 function must be agrin-independent.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C87 accurately summarize published literature on LRP4 function and provide appropriate context for the current study. The citations are appropriate and the inference about agrin-independence in Drosophila (C87) is logical given the absence of clear homologues.

results.result: The study concludes that LRP4 functions through SRPK79D, preferentially in excitatory neurons, and may represent a conserved synaptic organizer functioning presynaptically, cell autonomously, and independently of agrin.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 represent summary conclusions that are well-supported by the experimental data. The characterization as 'may represent' (C91) appropriately acknowledges that conservation to mammals remains to be fully tested.

results.result: lrp4dalek mutants are viable with slightly reduced body size.
results.evaluation: Claim C92 is a straightforward observation from maintaining mutant stocks. The viability is important for the functional studies performed.

results.result: Protein retention expansion microscopy achieves approximately 4-fold isotropic expansion of Drosophila CNS tissue.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3. This methodological validation is important for the high-resolution localization studies.

results.result: Prior work has established SRPK79D's role at the NMJ and LRP4's involvement in human diseases including ALS and myasthenia gravis.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 accurately cite published literature providing context for the clinical relevance of the findings. The citations are appropriate.

results.result: The antennal lobe is an established model circuit for sensory processing with well-characterized synaptic organization, and fluorescent marker methods are consistent with electron microscopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101 provide methodological context and validation, appropriately citing published work. This establishes the suitability of the experimental system.

results.result: Imbalances in excitation and inhibition are associated with epilepsy, social dysfunction, and potentially autism spectrum disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 accurately cite published literature on excitation/inhibition balance and neurological disorders. The claim about autism (C104) is appropriately qualified as 'may underlie.'

results.result: Prior work has identified various postsynaptic organizers that distinguish excitatory from inhibitory synapses, but presynaptic determinants are less well understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 accurately summarize published literature on synaptic organizers, providing context for the novelty of identifying a presynaptic excitatory-specific organizer.

results.result: In the mouse CNS, LRP4 regulates synaptic function and behavior, with localization to both pre- and postsynaptic compartments. The current work is the first to demonstrate clear cell-autonomous presynaptic functions, and the agrin-independence and excitatory specificity may be conserved.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C116 appropriately cite prior work on mammalian LRP4 and make reasonable claims about the novelty of the current findings (C114) and potential conservation (C115-C116). The comparison to mouse data (C116) strengthens the evolutionary argument.

results.result: Mammalian SRPK homologues are widely expressed in the brain and regulate spliceosome assembly, but have not been studied in mammalian synapse formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 accurately cite published literature on SRPKs and identify a gap in knowledge, providing rationale for future studies.
